reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive segmental progeroid syndrome caused by loss-of-function variants in the WRN RecQ helicase gene, leading to genomic instability
Development is normal until adolescence, when the pubertal growth spurt is absent and short stature becomes apparent
Characteristic features emerge in the twenties to thirties: premature greying and hair loss, scleroderma-like tight skin, a beaked nose and a high-pitched voice
Bilateral cataracts, often developing at an unusually young age, are a hallmark finding
Patients develop early-onset atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis and hypogonadism
There is a markedly raised risk of malignancy, with an unusual predominance of sarcomas (soft-tissue and osteosarcoma) alongside melanoma and thyroid cancer
Chronic, poorly healing skin ulcers around the ankles and over the Achilles tendon are typical and difficult to manage
Diagnosis rests on the combination of cardinal clinical features supported by molecular confirmation of biallelic WRN variants
reference.pathophysiology: Werner syndrome arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in WRN, which encodes a member of the RecQ family of DNA helicases with additional exonuclease activity. The protein participates in DNA replication, repair, recombination and telomere maintenance. Its loss produces genomic instability, accelerated telomere attrition and premature cellular senescence, which underlie the segmental (partial) acceleration of ageing phenotypes and the predisposition to cancer seen in affected individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Other RecQ helicase disorders such as Bloom and Rothmund-Thomson syndromes
Metabolic syndrome with early diabetes and premature atherosclerosis
Constitutional cataract with unrelated systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for biallelic WRN variants
Slit-lamp ophthalmological assessment for premature bilateral cataract
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile to detect diabetes and dyslipidaemia
Cardiovascular assessment for premature atherosclerotic disease
Age-appropriate malignancy surveillance with a low threshold for imaging or biopsy of new masses
redFlags: New or enlarging soft-tissue or bony mass suggesting sarcoma
Non-healing lower-limb ulcer with signs of secondary infection or malignant transformation
Symptoms of premature myocardial infarction or stroke
Rapid visual deterioration from advancing cataract
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is shortened, with most affected individuals dying in the fifth to sixth decade, predominantly from malignancy or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Careful metabolic control, cardiovascular risk reduction and cancer surveillance may improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing the scleroderma-like skin changes to systemic sclerosis and missing the progeroid diagnosis
Overlooking the characteristically young age of cataract onset
Failing to maintain vigilant malignancy surveillance, particularly for sarcomas
Underestimating premature cardiovascular and diabetic complications in a relatively young patient
management: With no treatment for the underlying helicase defect, target care at aggressive management of the premature age-related complications
Reduce cardiovascular risk intensively with statins, blood-pressure control, antiplatelet therapy and smoking cessation for early atherosclerosis
Manage type 2 diabetes mellitus with dietary measures and agents such as metformin or insulin, and treat associated dyslipidaemia
Treat osteoporosis with bisphosphonates alongside calcium and vitamin D
Refer for cataract surgery, and provide specialist wound care for the chronic, poorly healing lower-limb ulcers
Maintain heightened cancer surveillance given the raised risk, with a low threshold to image or biopsy any new mass, particularly for sarcoma, melanoma and thyroid cancer
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition and coordinate multidisciplinary care across the affected systems
